content: Bangungot, also known as Sudden Unexpected Death Syndrome (SUDS), refers to the sudden and unexplained death of adolescents and adults during sleep. This phenomenon is called bangungot in the Philippines, lai tai in Thailand, and hukuri in Japan. It is rarely observed in Western countries but is more commonly reported among young men in East and Southeast Asia. The term bangungot originates from the Tagalog word meaning bad dream. Survivors of bangungot often describe experiencing vivid dreams of falling into a bottomless pit. During these episodes, the individual is aware that they are dreaming but feels paralyzed, unable to move or wake up. SUDS has historically been surrounded by superstition. In Thailand, it is believed to be associated with eating rice cakes, while in the Philippines, it is thought that consuming large amounts of carbohydrates before sleeping can trigger bangungot. However, scientific understanding of this syndrome has only recently begun to develop. Victims of bangungot do not typically have any underlying organic heart diseases or structural abnormalities of the heart. However, during SUDS episodes, cardiac activity often shows irregular heart rhythms, including ventricular fibrillation. Survival depends on whether the heart rhythm spontaneously returns to normal. In the Philippines, traditional advice suggests wiggling the big toe during such episodes to snap back to consciousness. Ongoing genetic research, led by Spanish electrophysiologist Dr. Josep Brugada Terradellas, has identified mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene as a cause of SUDS. This genetic mutation is chromosomal in nature, which explains why the condition tends to run in families. Physicians recommend that individuals with a family history of SUDS consult a cardiologist for evaluation. In the Philippines, many cases of bangungot have been linked to Acute Hemorrhagic Pancreatitis. In contrast, in Thailand and Laos, SUDS is often associated with Brugada syndrome, a genetic condition affecting the heart's electrical system. Culturally, bangungot is also depicted in Philippine mythology as a creature called the batibat. This hag-like entity is said to sit on the victim's face, immobilizing and suffocating them during sleep.
